Hi!

3 questions:

  • How has internet communications been handled in times of war? Are they blocking some of the traffic to and from, to minimize the risk of their people being exposed to the enemies' views?

  • What do you realistically think would happen if a war broke out between two western countries? Let's say Ireland vs Norway for some reason. Do you think any of the countries would attempt to block all incoming and outgoing internet traffic between the two countries?

  • What do you realistically think would happen with internet communications within a country if an uprising broke out within a western country ("the masses" vs the establishment)? Is the internet something you can regulate if you have the resources (like how you can regulate a huge crowd of people with a small amount of people, if the small amount of people have the right equipment), or would it be impossible for the establishment, regardless of resources, to control the internet?
How has internet communications been handled between countries in times of war?

This may not be a particularly satisfactory answer, but I'll try!

The main issue with attempting to cordon the Internet in that way is part of the Internet's design - consider that when a series of packets is sent from one node to another, these packets will take any and every route they can use. Faster routes will attract a higher proportion of those packets, though slower routes will always still carry some of that message because they still represent useful capacity to shift data around, and TCP is built to handle communications where the packets may not arrive in order (or at all). I like to think that a good analogy is resistance in an electric circuit, where if there are two routes with resistances 1 ohm and 2 ohms, then they will carry 2/3 and 1/3 of the energy respectively (alternatively, if you've done any decision mathematics then you may be familiar with 'maximum flows' and 'minimum cuts').

The point here is that if any functional link is made between the inside and outside of a country, the packets can and will flow immediately. A state government can do quite a lot to prevent that, but it will only succeed if it achieved complete isolation, which I would rate as difficult at best or nearly impossible if there are people on either side who are determined to communicate with the other. It is important to note that people on the outside will be trying to make inward contact as well, and in the age of digital radio communications, there is no more 'one way'. It is a physical fact that if a strong signal (or accurately-pointed high-gain antenna) can be used to influence the electromagnetic field around a weak antenna for sending a message, then it is also able to sense such modulation for receiving a reply. With antennas, if you have a louder voice, you also have a more sensitive ear. To stop such signals, the state would have to jam them both spatially and spectrally - all frequencies at all angles of incidence at all places in the country, and that's before one even mentions trying to close off all existing physical cabled connections and prevent the construction of new ones.

In any case, your Ireland and/or Norway would have to shut off all communication to all countries. If a link leaks into the UK (noting Northern Ireland!) then leaks from there into France, it could take a multitude of routes around Europe to enter Norway from the south, the massive border with Sweden, or (if I recall) the small point which touches Finland and Russia. Even if the UK-France leak is closed somehow, note that there are under-sea cable connections between the UK and north America, and between mainland Norway and the island of Svalbard - where both NA and Svalbard are in simultaneous line-of-sight of satellites over the north pole (and Svalbard has an extensive array of satellite ground stations). With the proper equipment, pointing an antenna at a satellite is exactly like plugging in an Ethernet cable as far as IP networking is concerned; I've witnessed this personally. I imagine there are many other ways to establish a link, and the state would have the improbable tasks of thinking of all of them and preventing all of them.

Such management of the Internet, in its current form, is something of which we have a bare few examples. North Korea attempts it, though it's still possible to get mobile devices into NK and get a workable signal if close enough to SK, at least enough to produce the occasional deserter among those in NK who know but have to pretend they don't. Russia and China both have different extents of 'walled garden', though there's much less pretence there, to the point that servers around the world have to block thousands of Chinese attempts to find open proxies every day (both from citizens trying to see outside, and the government trying to locate and prevent access to them). The uprising in Egypt a few years ago was a great example of determination in an environment of censorship, which had activists such as Jacob Appelbaum working to maintain information flowing in and out via Twitter. We know that internal uprisings are helped greatly by access to the outside, so any state facing an uprising would certainly have to block as much as possible (both physically and by poisoning DNSs*), but this can only buy time. The uprising would either have to end in victory or be defeated by other means; the censorship is a temporary measure (though advisable/necessary, from the state's perspective).

In the case of war, the key consideration would be propaganda. Both sides would be so keenly determined to broadcast to the other that we would have the same situation as above, but with the resources of entire nations doing it, and they won't shut down internal communications because they need functional domestic propaganda as well. The issue of encryption** would also be interesting; at the moment, and by my judgment, the systematic shutting-down of various 'undesirable' tools/services such as Lavabit and TrueCrypt has continued long enough to suggest that such acts are not a double-bluff and that existing keypair encryption/authentication probably hasn't been broken mathematically or computationally (only by threats at gunpoint). There will be encryption smears in the media and attempts to outlaw civilian encryption (well, more smears and outlaw attempts than there are at the moment), though these are frivolous and impractical for the simple reason that an encrypted file is indistinguishable from a compressed file, in that either are indistinguishable from random numbers. As for the general communications, naturally the international links would be maintained for discussion between governments; either side would still be able to negotiate some sort of holdout cease-fire, truce, or treaty when it benefits them to do so. Ready to be broken similarly, of course - peace is, after all, a lie.

*Obviously DNS-tampering is only soft censorship in that it doesn't actually prevent access to the servers being 'censored', though the general public's reliance on DNS as a convenience feature is enough of a weakness to make it worth doing.

**Various militaries do use one-time pads for complete protection, and I imagine they treat unspent 1TPs the same way they would treat a stockpile of weapons. This will probably remain the case regardless of how many bits can be used in keypairs, for as long as the pads can still be distributed securely.
